If a decision set is lower-dimensional in an ambient Euclidean space, take $\mathbb R^d$ to be orthonormal affine coordinates on its affine hull (the smallest affine subspace containing it); thus interior, gradients, Hessians, and norms are relative to that affine hull. A **mirror regularizer** on $(K,U)$ is a real-valued function $R$ on $K\cup U$ that is continuous on $K$, twice continuously differentiable on $U$, agrees on $K\cap U$, and has symmetric positive-definite Hessian $H_R(z):=\nabla^2R(z)$ for every $z\in U$. We call $R$ $m$-strongly convex on $K$ in the Euclidean norm if, for some $m>0$, all $x,y\in K$ and $\lambda\in[0,1]$ satisfy

$$R((1-\lambda)x+\lambda y)\le (1-\lambda)R(x)+\lambda R(y)-\frac m2\lambda(1-\lambda)\|x-y\|_2^2.$$

For $x\in K\cup U$ and $y\in U$, the **Bregman divergence** generated by $R$ is

$$B_R(x\|y):=R(x)-R(y)-\langle\nabla R(y),x-y\rangle.$$

For $z\in U$ and vectors $v,h\in\mathbb R^d$, define the squared **local primal norm** and **local dual norm** by

$$\|v\|_z^2:=v^\top H_R(z)v,\qquad \|h\|_{*,z}^2:=h^\top H_R(z)^{-1}h.$$

By [F1], the remainder identity gives $B_R(x\|y)=\frac12(x-y)^\top H_R(y+\theta(x-y))(x-y)>0$, because the Hessian is positive definite and $x-y\ne0$. If $x=y$, the defining formula gives $B_R(x\|y)=0$. Thus the first claim holds.

Let $V$ be a finite-dimensional real inner product space and let $T:V\to V$ be
self-adjoint. Then $V$ has an orthonormal basis consisting of eigenvectors of
$T$.

Let $T:V\to W$ be a linear map between finite-dimensional inner product spaces. In orthonormal bases $\mathcal E=(e_j)$ of $V$ and $\mathcal F=(f_i)$ of $W$,

$$[T^*]_{\mathcal E\leftarrow\mathcal F}=\overline{[T]_{\mathcal F\leftarrow\mathcal E}}^{\mathsf T}.$$

Over $\mathbb R$ this is the transpose. The statement includes zero-sized bases.

Let $F$ be a field, let $m,n,p\in\mathbb N$, and let
$A=(a_{ij})\in M_{m\times n}(F)$ and
$B=(b_{jk})\in M_{n\times p}(F)$. Their **matrix product** is the matrix
$AB\in M_{m\times p}(F)$ whose entries are

$$(AB)_{ik}:=\sum_{j\in n}a_{ij}b_{jk}.$$

The sum is the finite sum in the additive commutative monoid of $F$. If $n=0$,
it is the empty sum, so $AB$ is the zero matrix of shape $m$ by $p$.

The **identity matrix** $I_n\in M_n(F)$ has entry $1$ when $i=j$ and entry $0$
when $i\ne j$. In particular, $I_0$ is the unique empty matrix in $M_0(F)$.

Let $F$ be a complete ordered field ([[def-complete-ordered-field]]). Then every
$a \in F$ with $a \ge 0$ has a **unique** $s \in F$ with $s \ge 0$ and $s^2 = a$;
we write $s = \sqrt{a}$. Consequently the positive elements of $F$ are exactly the
nonzero squares: $x > 0$ if and only if $x = y^2$ for some $y \neq 0$.

Let $n \in \mathbb{N}$. A natural number is a von Neumann natural, that is a set,
and $n = \{0, 1, \dots, n-1\}$ ([[def-natural-numbers]],
[[lem-nat-order-is-membership]]), so

$$\mathbb{R}^{n} \;=\; \{\, x \;:\; x \text{ is a function } n \to \mathbb{R} \,\}$$

is the function space of [[def-function-space]] at $F = \mathbb{R}$ and $X = n$,
a vector space over $\mathbb{R}$ under the pointwise operations
([[def-vector-space]]). We write $x_k := x(k)$ for $k < n$, and two elements of
$\mathbb{R}^{n}$ are equal exactly when they agree at every $k < n$. This is the
same set that [[lem-metrics-on-rn]] calls $\mathbb{R}^{n}$.

The **Euclidean inner product** of $x, y \in \mathbb{R}^{n}$ is the real number

$$\langle x, y\rangle \;:=\; \sum_{k<n} x_k\,y_k ,$$

the finite sum of [[def-finite-sum]] applied to the list $k \mapsto x_k y_k$
(extended by $0$ beyond $n$, as every finite list in this library is). The
**Euclidean norm** of $x$ is

$$\lVert x\rVert_2 \;:=\; \sqrt{\langle x, x\rangle},$$

which is defined because $\langle x,x\rangle = \sum_{k<n} x_k^{2} \ge 0$ (a sum
of nonnegative terms, [[lem-finite-sum-laws]] clause 4 and
[[lem-of-square-positive]], the case $x_k = 0$ giving $x_k^2 = 0$ by
[[def-integer-power]]) and every nonnegative real has a unique nonnegative square
root ([[thm-of-square-roots]]).

### Both are defined for every $n$, including $n = 0$

At $n = 0$ the set $\mathbb{R}^{0}$ has exactly one element, the empty function,
and it is the zero vector space ([[lem-standard-basis-of-f-n]] clause 5); the sum
above is the empty sum, so $\langle x,y\rangle = 0$ and $\lVert x\rVert_2 = 0$.
**This is the first place on this page where the two index regimes diverge, and
the divergence is deliberate.** The published metrics $d_1$, $d_2$, $d_\infty$ of
[[lem-metrics-on-rn]] are defined only for $n \ge 1$, because $d_\infty$ would
otherwise be a maximum over the empty index set; the algebra above needs no such
restriction. The boundary in this page runs between the algebra and the metric,
not where a reader would guess, and [[rem-rn-conventions-and-scope]] lists
exactly which items inherit $n \ge 1$.

### The algebra of the inner product

For all $x, y, z \in \mathbb{R}^{n}$ and $\lambda \in \mathbb{R}$:

1. **Symmetry.** $\langle x,y\rangle = \langle y,x\rangle$, since $x_ky_k = y_kx_k$
   termwise.
2. **Additivity in the first argument.**
   $\langle x + y, z\rangle = \langle x,z\rangle + \langle y,z\rangle$: the list
   $k \mapsto (x_k+y_k)z_k$ is the termwise sum of $k \mapsto x_kz_k$ and
   $k \mapsto y_kz_k$, so [[lem-finite-sum-laws]] clause 1 applies.
3. **Homogeneity in the first argument.**
   $\langle \lambda x, y\rangle = \lambda\langle x,y\rangle$, by
   [[lem-finite-sum-laws]] clause 2.
4. **Bilinearity.** Clauses 2 and 3 together with symmetry give the same two laws
   in the second argument.
5. **Positive definiteness.** $\langle x,x\rangle \ge 0$, and
   $\langle x,x\rangle = 0$ if and only if $x = 0$. Indeed a vanishing sum of
   nonnegative terms has every term $0$ ([[lem-finite-sum-laws]] clause 4), so
   $x_k^{2} = 0$ for every $k < n$, and a nonzero real has a positive square
   ([[lem-of-square-positive]]), whence $x_k = 0$ for every $k < n$ and $x = 0$.
6. **Agreement with the published Euclidean metric.** For $n \ge 1$ and
   $x, y \in \mathbb{R}^{n}$,
   $\lVert x - y\rVert_2 = \sqrt{\sum_{k<n}(x_k-y_k)^{2}} = d_2(x,y)$, the two
   sides being the same expression ([[lem-metrics-on-rn]]). In particular
   $\lVert x\rVert_2 = d_2(x, 0)$.

That $\lVert\cdot\rVert_2$ is a norm in the sense of [[def-norm-and-normed-space]]
is proved in [[thm-cauchy-schwarz-and-the-euclidean-norm]], where the triangle
inequality is obtained from the Cauchy-Schwarz inequality; it is not assumed
here.

Matrix multiplication over a field is associative and unital, distributes over
entrywise addition on both sides, and is compatible with scalar multiplication.
Precisely, whenever the displayed products have compatible shapes,

$$A(BC)=(AB)C,\qquad I_mA=A=AI_n,$$

$$(A+A')B=AB+A'B,\qquad A(B+B')=AB+AB',$$

$$0B=0=A0,\qquad (\lambda A)B=\lambda(AB)=A(\lambda B).$$

These identities include every zero-sized shape.

derivations.claim: By [F1, F2], choose an orthogonal matrix $Q$ whose columns are an orthonormal eigenbasis of $G$, so $G=Q\operatorname{diag}(\lambda_1,\ldots,\lambda_d)Q^\top$. For each unit eigenvector $q_i$, $\lambda_i=q_i^\top Gq_i\ge0$ by [A1].

Let $S$ be any symmetric positive-semidefinite matrix with $S^2=G$. By [F6], $SG=SS^2=S^3=S^2S=GS$, so $S$ preserves every eigenspace $E_\lambda(G)$: if $Gv=\lambda v$, then $G(Sv)=S(Gv)=\lambda Sv$. Its restriction to each $E_\lambda(G)$ is symmetric and positive semidefinite. By [F1, F2] that restriction has an orthonormal eigenbasis; each eigenvalue $\mu$ satisfies $\mu\ge0$ and $\mu^2=\lambda$, hence [F4] forces $\mu=\sqrt\lambda$. Therefore $S=\sqrt\lambda I$ on each $E_\lambda(G)$.

By [F4], choose $r_i=\sqrt{\lambda_i}\ge0$ with $r_i^2=\lambda_i$, and set $H=Q\operatorname{diag}(r_1,\ldots,r_d)Q^\top$. This matrix is symmetric and, using [F6] and $Q^\top Q=I$, $H^2=Q\operatorname{diag}(\lambda_1,\ldots,\lambda_d)Q^\top=G$. For every $v$, $v^\top Hv=\sum_i r_i(q_i^\top v)^2\ge0$, so $H$ is positive semidefinite.
The eigenspaces in step 1.1 form an orthogonal basis of $\mathbb R^d$, and step 1.2 shows that $S$ and $H$ act identically on every vector in that basis. Hence $S=H$, proving uniqueness.

Let $A \subseteq \mathbb{R}$, let $c \in A$ be a limit point of $A$
([[def-limit-point-r]]), let $f, g : A \to \mathbb{R}$ be differentiable at $c$
([[def-derivative]]) and let $\alpha \in \mathbb{R}$. Then:

1. $f + g$ is differentiable at $c$ and $(f+g)'(c) = f'(c) + g'(c)$;
2. $\alpha f$ is differentiable at $c$ and $(\alpha f)'(c) = \alpha f'(c)$;
3. $fg$ is differentiable at $c$ and $(fg)'(c) = f'(c)g(c) + f(c)g'(c)$;
4. if $g(c) \ne 0$ then, writing $A_0 := \{\, x \in A : g(x) \ne 0 \,\}$, the
   point $c$ lies in $A_0$ and is a limit point of $A_0$, the quotient
   $(f/g)|_{A_0} : A_0 \to \mathbb{R}$, $x \mapsto f(x)/g(x)$, is differentiable
   at $c$ as a function on $A_0$, and
   $$\bigl((f/g)|_{A_0}\bigr)'(c) \;=\; \frac{f'(c)\,g(c) - f(c)\,g'(c)}{g(c)^{2}} .$$

Each claim asserts two things: that the derivative on the left exists, and that
it has the stated value. Both are proved.

**Why claim 4 is stated on $A_0$.** The function $f/g$ is not defined where $g$
vanishes, and $g$ may vanish at points of $A$ far from $c$; restricting to $A_0$
is forced. That the restriction still has $c$ as a limit point, so that a
derivative there means anything at all, is not free either, and it is the last
claim of [[lem-sign-preservation-near-a-limit]] applied to $g$. The hypothesis
is $g(c) \ne 0$, not "$g$ vanishes nowhere".

**Everything is proved through
[[thm-caratheodory-characterisation]].** No difference quotient is estimated and
no limit theorem beyond continuity is used, so no choice principle is spent.
The four identities are four algebraic rearrangements of an increment, each
followed by a reading of [[thm-algebra-of-continuous-functions]].

Let $A, B \subseteq \mathbb{R}$, let $g : A \to \mathbb{R}$ with
$g[A] \subseteq B$ and let $f : B \to \mathbb{R}$, so that the composite
$f \circ g : A \to \mathbb{R}$ is defined. Let $c \in A$ be a limit point of
$A$ ([[def-limit-point-r]]) at which $g$ is differentiable
([[def-derivative]]), put $b := g(c)$, and suppose $b$ is a limit point of $B$
at which $f$ is differentiable. Then $f \circ g$ is differentiable at $c$ and

$$(f \circ g)'(c) \;=\; f'\bigl(g(c)\bigr)\,g'(c) .$$

**Both limit-point hypotheses are needed, and neither is automatic.** That $c$
is a limit point of $A$ is what makes $g'(c)$ and $(f \circ g)'(c)$ defined
symbols; that $b = g(c)$ is a limit point of $B$ is what makes $f'(b)$ one.
Nothing forces the second: $g$ may be differentiable at $c$ and send $c$ to an
isolated point of $B$, and there $f'(b)$ is not defined and the formula asserts
nothing.

**No case analysis appears anywhere.** The naive difference-quotient proof
writes $\frac{f(g(x)) - f(g(c))}{g(x) - g(c)} \cdot \frac{g(x) - g(c)}{x - c}$
and then has to say what happens where $g(x) = g(c)$, which may occur at points
arbitrarily close to $c$. Carathéodory's factorisation never divides by the
inner increment, so the difficulty does not arise.

Let $f:C\to\mathbb R$ be convex. For a positive finite family of points in $C$ and nonnegative weights summing to one, $f$ of their weighted Euclidean sum is at most the weighted sum of their $f$-values. Explicitly, if $N\ge1$, $x_1,\ldots,x_N\in C$, $\lambda_j\ge0$, and $\sum_{j=1}^N\lambda_j=1$, then

On the interior, differentiation using [F2, F3] gives $\partial_iR=\log q_i-\log p_n$ and $\nabla^2R(q)=\operatorname{diag}(1/q_1,\ldots,1/q_{n-1})+\frac1{p_n}\mathbf1\mathbf1^\top$. Since $0<q_i\le1$ and $p_n>0$, $v^\top(\nabla^2R(q)-I)v=\sum_{i<n}(1/q_i-1)v_i^2+(\sum_{i<n}v_i)^2/p_n\ge0$.

For interior $q,r$, [F8] keeps $(1-s)q+sr$ in $K_n$. The restriction $s\mapsto R((1-s)q+sr)-\frac12\|(1-s)q+sr\|_2^2$ has nonnegative second derivative on $0<s<1$ by step 1.2, hence is convex there by [F6]; continuity extends its convexity inequality to $s=0,1$. $$G_t=G_{t-1}+g_tg_t^\top=\sum_{s=1}^t g_sg_s^\top.$$

The accumulated matrix $G_t$ is symmetric and positive semidefinite. Choose either the **full-matrix scale** $H_t=G_t^{1/2}$, the unique positive-semidefinite square root, or the **diagonal scale** $H_t=\operatorname{diag}(\sqrt{(G_t)_{11}},\ldots,\sqrt{(G_t)_{dd}})$. Define $H_t^\dagger$ to be the Moore–Penrose pseudoinverse and update

$$y_{t+1}=x_t-\eta H_t^\dagger g_t,\qquad x_{t+1}\in\arg\min_{x\in K}(x-y_{t+1})^\top H_t(x-y_{t+1}).$$

A minimizer exists; if it is not unique, select any minimizer. Return $x_1,\ldots,x_T$. The matrix seminorm notation in the objective means $\|v\|_{H_t}^2=v^\top H_tv$. Let $n \in \mathbb{N}$. A natural number is a von Neumann natural, that is a set,
and $n = \{0, 1, \dots, n-1\}$ ([[def-natural-numbers]],
[[lem-nat-order-is-membership]]), so

$$\mathbb{R}^{n} \;=\; \{\, x \;:\; x \text{ is a function } n \to \mathbb{R} \,\}$$

is the function space of [[def-function-space]] at $F = \mathbb{R}$ and $X = n$,
a vector space over $\mathbb{R}$ under the pointwise operations
([[def-vector-space]]). We write $x_k := x(k)$ for $k < n$, and two elements of
$\mathbb{R}^{n}$ are equal exactly when they agree at every $k < n$. This is the
same set that [[lem-metrics-on-rn]] calls $\mathbb{R}^{n}$.

The **Euclidean inner product** of $x, y \in \mathbb{R}^{n}$ is the real number

$$\langle x, y\rangle \;:=\; \sum_{k<n} x_k\,y_k ,$$

the finite sum of [[def-finite-sum]] applied to the list $k \mapsto x_k y_k$
(extended by $0$ beyond $n$, as every finite list in this library is). The
**Euclidean norm** of $x$ is

$$\lVert x\rVert_2 \;:=\; \sqrt{\langle x, x\rangle},$$

which is defined because $\langle x,x\rangle = \sum_{k<n} x_k^{2} \ge 0$ (a sum
of nonnegative terms, [[lem-finite-sum-laws]] clause 4 and
[[lem-of-square-positive]], the case $x_k = 0$ giving $x_k^2 = 0$ by
[[def-integer-power]]) and every nonnegative real has a unique nonnegative square
root ([[thm-of-square-roots]]).

### Both are defined for every $n$, including $n = 0$

At $n = 0$ the set $\mathbb{R}^{0}$ has exactly one element, the empty function,
and it is the zero vector space ([[lem-standard-basis-of-f-n]] clause 5); the sum
above is the empty sum, so $\langle x,y\rangle = 0$ and $\lVert x\rVert_2 = 0$.
**This is the first place on this page where the two index regimes diverge, and
the divergence is deliberate.** The published metrics $d_1$, $d_2$, $d_\infty$ of
[[lem-metrics-on-rn]] are defined only for $n \ge 1$, because $d_\infty$ would
otherwise be a maximum over the empty index set; the algebra above needs no such
restriction. The boundary in this page runs between the algebra and the metric,
not where a reader would guess, and [[rem-rn-conventions-and-scope]] lists
exactly which items inherit $n \ge 1$.

### The algebra of the inner product

For all $x, y, z \in \mathbb{R}^{n}$ and $\lambda \in \mathbb{R}$:

1. **Symmetry.** $\langle x,y\rangle = \langle y,x\rangle$, since $x_ky_k = y_kx_k$
   termwise.
2. **Additivity in the first argument.**
   $\langle x + y, z\rangle = \langle x,z\rangle + \langle y,z\rangle$: the list
   $k \mapsto (x_k+y_k)z_k$ is the termwise sum of $k \mapsto x_kz_k$ and
   $k \mapsto y_kz_k$, so [[lem-finite-sum-laws]] clause 1 applies.
3. **Homogeneity in the first argument.**
   $\langle \lambda x, y\rangle = \lambda\langle x,y\rangle$, by
   [[lem-finite-sum-laws]] clause 2.
4. **Bilinearity.** Clauses 2 and 3 together with symmetry give the same two laws
   in the second argument.
5. **Positive definiteness.** $\langle x,x\rangle \ge 0$, and
   $\langle x,x\rangle = 0$ if and only if $x = 0$. Indeed a vanishing sum of
   nonnegative terms has every term $0$ ([[lem-finite-sum-laws]] clause 4), so
   $x_k^{2} = 0$ for every $k < n$, and a nonzero real has a positive square
   ([[lem-of-square-positive]]), whence $x_k = 0$ for every $k < n$ and $x = 0$.
6. **Agreement with the published Euclidean metric.** For $n \ge 1$ and
   $x, y \in \mathbb{R}^{n}$,
   $\lVert x - y\rVert_2 = \sqrt{\sum_{k<n}(x_k-y_k)^{2}} = d_2(x,y)$, the two
   sides being the same expression ([[lem-metrics-on-rn]]). In particular
   $\lVert x\rVert_2 = d_2(x, 0)$.

That $\lVert\cdot\rVert_2$ is a norm in the sense of [[def-norm-and-normed-space]]
is proved in [[thm-cauchy-schwarz-and-the-euclidean-norm]], where the triangle
inequality is obtained from the Cauchy-Schwarz inequality; it is not assumed
here.

Using the Euclidean metric and its balls ([[lem-metrics-on-rn]], [[def-metric-ball]]), $f$ is upper semicontinuous at $a$ when for every $\varepsilon>0$ there is $\delta>0$ such that $f(x)<f(a)+\varepsilon$ for every $x\in A\cap B_2(a,\delta)$.

The function is **lower semicontinuous at $a$** when for every $\varepsilon>0$ there is $\delta>0$ such that

$$f(a)-\varepsilon<f(x)\qquad(x\in A\cap B_2(a,\delta)).$$

It is upper or lower semicontinuous on $A$ when the corresponding condition holds at every point of $A$. These are relative notions on $A$; when $A$ is empty, each on-set condition is vacuous. A continuous function ([[def-metric-continuity]]) satisfies both conditions.

Using the Euclidean metric and its balls ([[lem-metrics-on-rn]], [[def-metric-ball]]), $f$ is upper semicontinuous at $a$ when for every $\varepsilon>0$ there is $\delta>0$ such that $f(x)<f(a)+\varepsilon$ for every $x\in A\cap B_2(a,\delta)$.

derivations.claim: By [F3], $K$ is compact. Continuity of $R$ on the nonempty set $K$ and [F7] make it lower semicontinuous; [F4] then implies that $R$ attains a minimum on $K$.

Since $x_+(y)$ minimizes $B_R(\cdot\|y)$, the right derivative at zero of $s\mapsto B_R(x_+(y)+s(u-x_+(y))\|y)$ is nonnegative. Differentiating its defining formula at $s=0$ gives $\langle\nabla R(x_+(y))-\nabla R(y),u-x_+(y)\rangle\ge0$.

If two distinct points minimized $R$, their midpoint would lie in $K$ by [F5]. The strong-convexity inequality at $\lambda=1/2$ would make its value at least $m\|x-y\|_2^2/8$ below the common minimum, a contradiction. Thus the minimizer is unique.

For fixed $y\in U$, the formula in [F2] writes $B_R(x\|y)$ as the continuous function $R(x)$ plus an affine function of $x$. It is therefore lower semicontinuous by [F7] and attains a minimum on compact $K$ by [F3, F4]. Let $d\ge1$, let $K\subseteq\mathbb R^d$ be a nonempty bounded closed convex set with nonempty interior, and let $U\subseteq\mathbb R^d$ be an open convex set such that $\operatorname{int}(K)\subseteq U$ and $K\subseteq\overline U$. If a decision set is lower-dimensional in an ambient Euclidean space, take $\mathbb R^d$ to be orthonormal affine coordinates on its affine hull (the smallest affine subspace containing it); thus interior, gradients, Hessians, and norms are relative to that affine hull. A **mirror regularizer** on $(K,U)$ is a real-valued function $R$ on $K\cup U$ that is continuous on $K$, twice continuously differentiable on $U$, agrees on $K\cap U$, and has symmetric positive-definite Hessian $H_R(z):=\nabla^2R(z)$ for every $z\in U$. We call $R$ $m$-strongly convex on $K$ in the Euclidean norm if, for some $m>0$, all $x,y\in K$ and $\lambda\in[0,1]$ satisfy

$$R((1-\lambda)x+\lambda y)\le (1-\lambda)R(x)+\lambda R(y)-\frac m2\lambda(1-\lambda)\|x-y\|_2^2.$$

For $x\in K\cup U$ and $y\in U$, the **Bregman divergence** generated by $R$ is

$$B_R(x\|y):=R(x)-R(y)-\langle\nabla R(y),x-y\rangle.$$

For $z\in U$ and vectors $v,h\in\mathbb R^d$, define the squared **local primal norm** and **local dual norm** by

$$\|v\|_z^2:=v^\top H_R(z)v,\qquad \|h\|_{*,z}^2:=h^\top H_R(z)^{-1}h.$$

Let $K\subseteq\mathbb R^d$, let $U\subseteq\mathbb R^d$ be open, and let $R$ be a mirror regularizer whose Bregman divergence is $B_R(x\|y)=R(x)-R(y)-\langle
abla R(y),x-yangle$ for $x\in K\cup U$ and $y\in U$. For $a\in K\cup U$ and $b,c\in U$,

$$\langle a-b,
abla R(c)-
abla R(b)angle=B_R(a\|b)-B_R(a\|c)+B_R(b\|c).$$

Let $(K,U,R)$ be a mirror regularizer, and suppose $R$ is $m$-strongly convex on $K$ for some $m>0$. For $x,y\in U$,

$$B_R(x\|y)\ge0,$$

with strict inequality when $x\ne y$. For $x\in K$ and $y\in K\cap U$,

$$B_R(x\|y)\ge\frac m2\|x-y\|_2^2.$$

Let $(K,U,R)$ be a mirror regularizer with $R$ $m$-strongly convex on $K$ for some $m>0$. Fix an integer horizon $T\ge1$ and a step size $\eta>0$. Admissibility requires the unique minimizer of $R$ on $K$ to lie in $U$; initialize $x_1$ at this minimizer. At each round $t=1,\ldots,T$, play $x_t$ before observing the full current loss $f_t$, with losses and gradients written in the same affine coordinates used for $K$. Use either of these feedback cases:

1. $f_t$ is differentiable and convex on an open convex set containing $K$, and $g_t=\nabla f_t(x_t)$.
2. $f_t$ is convex on a convex set containing $K$, and a supplied vector $g_t$ satisfies $f_t(u)\ge f_t(x_t)+\langle g_t,u-x_t\rangle$ for every $u\in K$.

For each round require that there is a unique $y_{t+1}\in U$ satisfying

$$\nabla R(y_{t+1})=\nabla R(x_t)-\eta g_t.$$

Set $x_{t+1}$ to the minimizer of $B_R(x\|y_{t+1})$ over $x\in K$, and require this minimizer to lie in $U$ so that the next dual update is defined. The Bregman minimizer exists and is unique under the stated strong-convexity and compactness hypotheses. Output the decisions $x_1,\ldots,x_T$; the final $x_{T+1}$ is the internal post-round iterate.

Let $d\ge1$, let $K\subseteq\mathbb R^d$ be nonempty, bounded, closed, and convex, and let $(K,U,R)$ be a mirror regularizer with $R$ $m$-strongly convex on $K$ for some $m>0$. Then $R$ has a unique minimizer on $K$, and for every $y\in U$ the function $x\mapsto B_R(x\|y)$ has a unique minimizer $x_+(y)$ on $K$. If $x_+(y)\in U$, then for every $u\in K$,

$$\langle\nabla R(x_+(y))-\nabla R(y),u-x_+(y)\rangle\ge0$$

and

$$B_R(u\|y)\ge B_R(u\|x_+(y))+B_R(x_+(y)\|y).$$

Let $U\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ be open and convex, and let $f:U\to\mathbb R$ be differentiable. Then $f$ is convex if and only if

$$f(y)\ge f(x)+\langle\nabla f(x),y-x\rangle\qquad(x,y\in U).$$

Equivalently, $\nabla f(x)$ is a subgradient at every $x$ ([[def-subgradient-and-subdifferential]], [[def-jacobian-matrix-and-gradient]]).

Let $f:C\to\mathbb R$ be convex on a convex set $C\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ ([[def-convex-and-strictly-convex-functions-on-euclidean-sets]]), and let $a\in C$. A vector $v$ is a subgradient of $f$ at $a$ when $f(y)\ge f(a)+\langle v,y-a\rangle$ for every $y$ in the domain.

The **subdifferential** is the set

$$\partial f(a):=\{v\in\mathbb R^n:f(y)\ge f(a)+\langle v,y-a\rangle\text{ for every }y\in C\},$$

with the Euclidean inner product of [[def-euclidean-inner-product]]. The definition permits $\partial f(a)$ to be empty or to contain more than one vector.

Let $k\in\mathbb N$, let $U\subseteq\mathbb R^m$ be open and convex, $a,a+h\in U$, and $f\in C^{k+1}(U)$. Write $\iota:\mathbb N\to\mathbb R$ for the canonical-natural map of [[def-multivariable-taylor-polynomial]]. Then some $\theta\in(0,1)$ satisfies

$$f(a+h)=T_kf(a;h)+\sum_{|\alpha|=k+1}\frac{D^\alpha f(a+\theta h)}{\iota(\alpha!)}h^\alpha.$$

Let a finite-horizon online protocol have horizon $T$, action set $K$, round losses $f_t:K\to\mathbb R$, and learner choices $x_t\in K$. Whenever a minimum below is used, assume it is finite and attained. For a fixed comparator $u\in K$, the realized regret is
$$
R_T(u):=\sum_{t=1}^T f_t(x_t)-\sum_{t=1}^T f_t(u).
$$
The **static regret** is
$$
R_T^{\rm stat}:=\sum_{t=1}^T f_t(x_t)-\min_{u\in K}\sum_{t=1}^T f_t(u).
$$
For randomized learners or environments, **expected regret** is the expectation of the specified regret random variable over their joint randomness, when that random variable is measurable and integrable. In a stochastic finite-arm reward model with means $(\mu_i)_{i\in[N]}$, let $\mu^*:=\max_{i\in[N]}\mu_i$. The **pseudo-regret** is the random variable
$$
\bar R_T:=\sum_{t=1}^T(\mu^*-\mu_{A_t}),
$$
whereas the **realized reward regret** is
$$
R_T^{\rm rew}:=\sum_{t=1}^T(\mu^*-Y_t).
$$

For dynamic comparators, suppose $K\subseteq\mathbb R^d$ for a positive integer $d$ and fix a norm $\|\cdot\|:\mathbb R^d\to[0,\infty)$, meaning $\|v\|=0$ exactly when $v=0$, $\|\lambda v\|=|\lambda|\|v\|$ for every $\lambda\in\mathbb R$, and $\|v+w\|\le\|v\|+\|w\|$. Given a comparator sequence $u_{1:T}=(u_1,\ldots,u_T)\in K^T$, the **dynamic regret** and its **path length** are
$$
R_T^{\rm dyn}(u_{1:T}):=\sum_{t=1}^T f_t(x_t)-\sum_{t=1}^T f_t(u_t),\qquad P(u_{1:T}):=1+\sum_{t=1}^{T-1}\|u_t-u_{t+1}\|.
$$
For a nonempty contiguous integer interval $I=[r,s]$ with $1\le r\le s\le T$, its **interval regret** is
$$
R_I:=\sum_{t=r}^s f_t(x_t)-\min_{u\in K}\sum_{t=r}^s f_t(u),
$$
and the **adaptive regret** is $\max_{1\le r\le s\le T}R_{[r,s]}$. For an algorithm $A$ producing the choices $x_1,\ldots,x_T$, write $R_I(A)$ for its interval regret on $I$. The algorithm is **strongly adaptive** relative to a specified loss, feedback, adversary, and comparator class only if there are a stated base algorithm $A_0$, constants $C>0$ and $p\ge0$, and a specified bound $B_{A_0}(n)$ on $A_0$'s static regret at horizon $n$ in that same class, such that for every nonempty contiguous interval $I\subseteq\{1,\ldots,T\}$,
$$
R_I(A)\le C\bigl(\log(eT)\bigr)^p B_{A_0}(|I|),
$$
where $\log$ is the natural logarithm and $|I|=s-r+1$. Strong adaptivity is a regret property relative to intervals; it does not imply anytime statistical validity.

Let $n \in \mathbb{N}$ with $n \ge 1$, let $\mathbb{R}^n$ be the set of functions
$n \to \mathbb{R}$ and let $d_2$ be the Euclidean metric on it
([[lem-metrics-on-rn]]). Then:

1. **Closed boxes are compact.** For reals $a_k \le b_k$ $(k < n)$ the box
   $Q = \{\, x \in \mathbb{R}^n : a_k \le x_k \le b_k \text{ for every } k < n \,\}$
   is a compact subset of $(\mathbb{R}^n, d_2)$ ([[def-metric-compactness]]).
2. **Heine-Borel.** A subset $K \subseteq \mathbb{R}^n$ is a compact subset of
   $(\mathbb{R}^n, d_2)$ if and only if $K$ is closed in $\mathbb{R}^n$
   ([[def-metric-topology]]) and bounded
   ([[def-metric-bounded-diameter]]).
3. **The real line.** A subset $K \subseteq \mathbb{R}$ is a compact subset of
   $(\mathbb{R}, d_{\mathbb{R}})$, the usual metric $d_{\mathbb{R}}(x,y) = |x-y|$
   ([[lem-real-line-is-a-metric-space]]), if and only if $K$ is closed in
   $\mathbb{R}$ and bounded.

**No choice principle is used.** The bisection below halves one coordinate at a
time and takes the **left** half whenever the left half still fails to be finitely
covered, the right half otherwise: a rule with two outcomes, decided by a
property of the box, not a selection. That is the whole reason the theorem is
available in ZF, while the general "complete and totally bounded implies compact"
([[thm-complete-and-totally-bounded-implies-compact]]) is not.

The hypothesis $n \ge 1$ is inherited from [[lem-metrics-on-rn]], which defines
$\mathbb{R}^n$ and its metrics only there; the last remark below records what
happens at $n = 0$.

Let $n\ge1$ and let $K\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ be nonempty and compact. Every lower semicontinuous function $f:K\to\mathbb R$ is bounded below and attains a minimum. Dually, every upper semicontinuous function $f:K\to\mathbb R$ is bounded above and attains a maximum.

A subset $U\subseteq\mathbb R^m$ is **convex** when, for all $x,y\in U$ and $t\in[0,1]$ ([[def-interval]]), the point $(1-t)x+ty$ lies in $U$. Thus the full line segment from $x$ to $y$ remains in $U$.

Let $C\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ be convex ([[def-convex-subset-of-euclidean-space]]). The function $f:C\to\mathbb R$ is convex when $f((1-t)x+ty)\le(1-t)f(x)+tf(y)$ for all $x,y\in C$ and $t\in[0,1]$. The parameter interval is the closed interval of [[def-interval]].

It is strictly convex when the inequality is strict for distinct $x,y$ and $0<t<1$. No strict inequality is required at $t=0$ or $t=1$, where the two sides coincide. The empty set and a singleton support convex functions, and strict convexity on either is vacuous.

Let $n \in \mathbb{N}$. A natural number is a von Neumann natural, that is a set,
and $n = \{0, 1, \dots, n-1\}$ ([[def-natural-numbers]],
[[lem-nat-order-is-membership]]), so

$$\mathbb{R}^{n} \;=\; \{\, x \;:\; x \text{ is a function } n \to \mathbb{R} \,\}$$

is the function space of [[def-function-space]] at $F = \mathbb{R}$ and $X = n$,
a vector space over $\mathbb{R}$ under the pointwise operations
([[def-vector-space]]). We write $x_k := x(k)$ for $k < n$, and two elements of
$\mathbb{R}^{n}$ are equal exactly when they agree at every $k < n$. This is the
same set that [[lem-metrics-on-rn]] calls $\mathbb{R}^{n}$.

The **Euclidean inner product** of $x, y \in \mathbb{R}^{n}$ is the real number

$$\langle x, y\rangle \;:=\; \sum_{k<n} x_k\,y_k ,$$

the finite sum of [[def-finite-sum]] applied to the list $k \mapsto x_k y_k$
(extended by $0$ beyond $n$, as every finite list in this library is). The
**Euclidean norm** of $x$ is

$$\lVert x\rVert_2 \;:=\; \sqrt{\langle x, x\rangle},$$

which is defined because $\langle x,x\rangle = \sum_{k<n} x_k^{2} \ge 0$ (a sum
of nonnegative terms, [[lem-finite-sum-laws]] clause 4 and
[[lem-of-square-positive]], the case $x_k = 0$ giving $x_k^2 = 0$ by
[[def-integer-power]]) and every nonnegative real has a unique nonnegative square
root ([[thm-of-square-roots]]).

### Both are defined for every $n$, including $n = 0$

At $n = 0$ the set $\mathbb{R}^{0}$ has exactly one element, the empty function,
and it is the zero vector space ([[lem-standard-basis-of-f-n]] clause 5); the sum
above is the empty sum, so $\langle x,y\rangle = 0$ and $\lVert x\rVert_2 = 0$.
**This is the first place on this page where the two index regimes diverge, and
the divergence is deliberate.** The published metrics $d_1$, $d_2$, $d_\infty$ of
[[lem-metrics-on-rn]] are defined only for $n \ge 1$, because $d_\infty$ would
otherwise be a maximum over the empty index set; the algebra above needs no such
restriction. The boundary in this page runs between the algebra and the metric,
not where a reader would guess, and [[rem-rn-conventions-and-scope]] lists
exactly which items inherit $n \ge 1$.

### The algebra of the inner product

For all $x, y, z \in \mathbb{R}^{n}$ and $\lambda \in \mathbb{R}$:

1. **Symmetry.** $\langle x,y\rangle = \langle y,x\rangle$, since $x_ky_k = y_kx_k$
   termwise.
2. **Additivity in the first argument.**
   $\langle x + y, z\rangle = \langle x,z\rangle + \langle y,z\rangle$: the list
   $k \mapsto (x_k+y_k)z_k$ is the termwise sum of $k \mapsto x_kz_k$ and
   $k \mapsto y_kz_k$, so [[lem-finite-sum-laws]] clause 1 applies.
3. **Homogeneity in the first argument.**
   $\langle \lambda x, y\rangle = \lambda\langle x,y\rangle$, by
   [[lem-finite-sum-laws]] clause 2.
4. **Bilinearity.** Clauses 2 and 3 together with symmetry give the same two laws
   in the second argument.
5. **Positive definiteness.** $\langle x,x\rangle \ge 0$, and
   $\langle x,x\rangle = 0$ if and only if $x = 0$. Indeed a vanishing sum of
   nonnegative terms has every term $0$ ([[lem-finite-sum-laws]] clause 4), so
   $x_k^{2} = 0$ for every $k < n$, and a nonzero real has a positive square
   ([[lem-of-square-positive]]), whence $x_k = 0$ for every $k < n$ and $x = 0$.
6. **Agreement with the published Euclidean metric.** For $n \ge 1$ and
   $x, y \in \mathbb{R}^{n}$,
   $\lVert x - y\rVert_2 = \sqrt{\sum_{k<n}(x_k-y_k)^{2}} = d_2(x,y)$, the two
   sides being the same expression ([[lem-metrics-on-rn]]). In particular
   $\lVert x\rVert_2 = d_2(x, 0)$.

That $\lVert\cdot\rVert_2$ is a norm in the sense of [[def-norm-and-normed-space]]
is proved in [[thm-cauchy-schwarz-and-the-euclidean-norm]], where the triangle
inequality is obtained from the Cauchy-Schwarz inequality; it is not assumed
here.

If every partial derivative $\partial_jf_i(a)$ of $f:U\to\mathbb R^n$ exists, the **Jacobian matrix** is $Jf(a)=(\partial_jf_i(a))_{i<n,j<m}$. For scalar-valued $f$, its **gradient** is

$$\nabla f(a):=(\partial_0f(a),\ldots,\partial_{m-1}f(a))\in\mathbb R^m,$$

with coordinates understood in the standard basis ([[lem-standard-basis-of-f-n]]). The partial derivatives are those of [[def-directional-and-partial-derivatives]].

derivations.claim: In either loss case [F6] or [F7] gives $f_t(x_t)-f_t(u)\le\langle g_t,x_t-u\rangle$ for every $u\in K$; the loss convexity convention is [F13], and gradients are the vectors in [F15].

Apply [F8] to $R$ along the segment from $x_t$ to $y_{t+1}$. If $x_t\ne y_{t+1}$ it gives $z_t=x_t+\theta_t(y_{t+1}-x_t)\in U$ and $B_R(y_{t+1}\|x_t)=\tfrac12(x_t-y_{t+1})^\top H_R(z_t)(x_t-y_{t+1})$; if the two points coincide, choose $z_t=x_t$ and both sides are zero. Thus the stated intermediate-point identity holds.
Put $d_t=x_t-y_{t+1}$. Expanding the two Bregman terms by [F1] gives $B_R(x_t\|y_{t+1})+B_R(y_{t+1}\|x_t)=\langle\nabla R(x_t)-\nabla R(y_{t+1}),d_t\rangle=\eta\langle g_t,d_t\rangle$ by [A1].

By [F10], $K$ is compact; by [F1], $R$ is continuous there; hence [F11] gives $M=\max_KR$ and $m_0=\min_KR$. Every difference $R(x)-R(y)$ is at most $M-m_0$, and points attaining $M$ and $m_0$ attain this difference, so $D_R^2=M-m_0$ is finite and nonnegative.

Let $A=H_R(z_t)$, $a=\|g_t\|_{*,z_t}$, and $b=\|d_t\|_{z_t}$. For every real $\lambda$, positive definiteness gives $0\le(d_t-\lambda A^{-1}g_t)^\top A(d_t-\lambda A^{-1}g_t)=b^2-2\lambda\langle g_t,d_t\rangle+\lambda^2a^2$, with the pairing from [F14]. If $a>0$, substitute $\lambda=\langle g_t,d_t\rangle/a^2$ to get $\langle g_t,d_t\rangle^2\le a^2b^2$; if $a=0$, positive definiteness of $A^{-1}$ forces $g_t=0$. In either case $\langle g_t,d_t\rangle\le ab$. By steps 1.2 and 1.3, $B_R(x_t\|y_{t+1})=\eta\langle g_t,d_t\rangle-b^2/2\le\eta ab-b^2/2\le\eta^2a^2/2$, the last inequality following from $(b-\eta a)^2\ge0$.

Use [F2] with $a=u$, $b=x_t$, and $c=y_{t+1}$, together with [A1], to write $\eta\langle g_t,x_t-u\rangle=B_R(u\|x_t)-B_R(u\|y_{t+1})+B_R(x_t\|y_{t+1})$. Apply [F5] to the middle potential and [F3] to $B_R(x_{t+1}\|y_{t+1})$; then apply step 2.1. With step 1.1 this gives $\eta(f_t(x_t)-f_t(u))\le B_R(u\|x_t)-B_R(u\|x_{t+1})+\frac{\eta^2}{2}\|g_t\|_{*,z_t}^2$.

Sum step 3.1 over $t$. The Bregman terms telescope, and [F3] gives $B_R(u\|x_{T+1})\ge0$ because $u\in K$ and $x_{T+1}\in K\cap U$. Divide by $\eta>0$ to obtain $R_T(u)\le B_R(u\|x_1)/\eta+(\eta/2)\sum_{t=1}^T\|g_t\|_{*,z_t}^2$.

For fixed $u\in K$, [F12] puts the segment $x_1+s(u-x_1)$ in $K$, and $R$ has a minimum at $s=0$. Since $x_1\in U$, the right derivative is $\langle\nabla R(x_1),u-x_1\rangle\ge0$. The Bregman identity gives $R(u)-R(x_1)=B_R(u\|x_1)+\langle\nabla R(x_1),u-x_1\rangle\ge B_R(u\|x_1)$. Substitute in step 4.1 to prove the pointwise bound.

For every $u\in K$, $R(u)-R(x_1)\le D_R^2$. Under [A4], step 5.1 gives $R_T(u)\le D_R^2/\eta+\eta TG_R^2/2$. Substituting $\eta=D_R/(G_R\sqrt T)$ gives $\tfrac32D_RG_R\sqrt T$. For arbitrary $\eta>0$, the difference between $D_R^2/\eta+\eta TG_R^2/2$ and $\sqrt2D_RG_R\sqrt T$ is $\left(D_R/\sqrt\eta-G_R\sqrt{T\eta/2}\right)^2\ge0$. Equality holds when $D_R^2/\eta=\eta TG_R^2/2$, that is, $\eta=\sqrt2D_R/(G_R\sqrt T)$. This proves the optimized corrected bound.

Let $A \subseteq \mathbb{R}$, let $c \in A$ be a limit point of $A$
([[def-limit-point-r]]), let $f, g : A \to \mathbb{R}$ be differentiable at $c$
([[def-derivative]]) and let $\alpha \in \mathbb{R}$. Then:

1. $f + g$ is differentiable at $c$ and $(f+g)'(c) = f'(c) + g'(c)$;
2. $\alpha f$ is differentiable at $c$ and $(\alpha f)'(c) = \alpha f'(c)$;
3. $fg$ is differentiable at $c$ and $(fg)'(c) = f'(c)g(c) + f(c)g'(c)$;
4. if $g(c) \ne 0$ then, writing $A_0 := \{\, x \in A : g(x) \ne 0 \,\}$, the
   point $c$ lies in $A_0$ and is a limit point of $A_0$, the quotient
   $(f/g)|_{A_0} : A_0 \to \mathbb{R}$, $x \mapsto f(x)/g(x)$, is differentiable
   at $c$ as a function on $A_0$, and
   $$\bigl((f/g)|_{A_0}\bigr)'(c) \;=\; \frac{f'(c)\,g(c) - f(c)\,g'(c)}{g(c)^{2}} .$$

Each claim asserts two things: that the derivative on the left exists, and that
it has the stated value. Both are proved.

**Why claim 4 is stated on $A_0$.** The function $f/g$ is not defined where $g$
vanishes, and $g$ may vanish at points of $A$ far from $c$; restricting to $A_0$
is forced. That the restriction still has $c$ as a limit point, so that a
derivative there means anything at all, is not free either, and it is the last
claim of [[lem-sign-preservation-near-a-limit]] applied to $g$. The hypothesis

**Everything is proved through
[[thm-caratheodory-characterisation]].** No difference quotient is estimated and
no limit theorem beyond continuity is used, so no choice principle is spent.
The four identities are four algebraic rearrangements of an increment, each

Let $d\ge1$, let $K\subseteq\mathbb R^d$ be a nonempty bounded closed convex set with nonempty interior, and let $U\subseteq\mathbb R^d$ be an open convex set such that $\operatorname{int}(K)\subseteq U$ and $K\subseteq\overline U$. If a decision set is lower-dimensional in an ambient Euclidean space, take $\mathbb R^d$ to be orthonormal affine coordinates on its affine hull (the smallest affine subspace containing it); thus interior, gradients, Hessians, and norms are relative to that affine hull. A **mirror regularizer** on $(K,U)$ is a real-valued function $R$ on $K\cup U$ that is continuous on $K$, twice continuously differentiable on $U$, agrees on $K\cap U$, and has symmetric positive-definite Hessian $H_R(z):=\nabla^2R(z)$ for every $z\in U$. We call $R$ $m$-strongly convex on $K$ in the Euclidean norm if, for some $m>0$, all $x,y\in K$ and $\lambda\in[0,1]$ satisfy

$$R((1-\lambda)x+\lambda y)\le (1-\lambda)R(x)+\lambda R(y)-\frac m2\lambda(1-\lambda)\|x-y\|_2^2.$$

For $x\in K\cup U$ and $y\in U$, the **Bregman divergence** generated by $R$ is

$$B_R(x\|y):=R(x)-R(y)-\langle\nabla R(y),x-y\rangle.$$

We call $R$ $m$-strongly convex on $K$ in the Euclidean norm if, for some $m>0$, all $x,y\in K$ and $\lambda\in[0,1]$ satisfy

$$R((1-\lambda)x+\lambda y)\le (1-\lambda)R(x)+\lambda R(y)-\frac m2\lambda(1-\lambda)\|x-y\|_2^2.$$

$$B_R(x\|y):=R(x)-R(y)-\langle\nabla R(y),x-y\rangle.$$

Let $d\ge1$ be an integer and let $K\subseteq\mathbb R^d$ be nonempty, bounded, closed, and convex; let $x_1\in K$, let $T\ge1$ be an integer, and fix a step size $\eta>0$. Coordinate and matrix-entry subscripts in this procedure are one-based labels: for $i,j\in\{1,\ldots,d\}$, write $g_i=g(i-1)$ and $G_{ij}=G(i-1,j-1)$ in the underlying zero-based Euclidean and matrix conventions, and use the same relabeling for the other vectors and matrices. Initialize $G_0=0$. For each round $t=1,\ldots,T$, play $x_t$, then receive the full current loss information and its prescribed gradient vector $g_t\in\mathbb R^d$, and set

$$G_t=G_{t-1}+g_tg_t^\top=\sum_{s=1}^t g_sg_s^\top.$$

The accumulated matrix $G_t$ is symmetric and positive semidefinite. Choose either the **full-matrix scale** $H_t=G_t^{1/2}$, the unique positive-semidefinite square root, or the **diagonal scale** $H_t=\operatorname{diag}(\sqrt{(G_t)_{11}},\ldots,\sqrt{(G_t)_{dd}})$. Define $H_t^\dagger$ to be the Moore–Penrose pseudoinverse and update

$$y_{t+1}=x_t-\eta H_t^\dagger g_t,\qquad x_{t+1}\in\arg\min_{x\in K}(x-y_{t+1})^\top H_t(x-y_{t+1}).$$

A minimizer exists; if it is not unique, select any minimizer. Return $x_1,\ldots,x_T$. The matrix seminorm notation in the objective means $\|v\|_{H_t}^2=v^\top H_tv$. The diagonal scale here is formed by taking each diagonal entry of $G_t$ and then its scalar square root; in general it is not $\operatorname{diag}(G_t^{1/2})$. This is an update definition only and asserts no regret bound.

Let $F$ be a field, let $m,n,p\in\mathbb N$, and let
$A=(a_{ij})\in M_{m\times n}(F)$ and
$B=(b_{jk})\in M_{n\times p}(F)$. Their **matrix product** is the matrix
$AB\in M_{m\times p}(F)$ whose entries are

$$(AB)_{ik}:=\sum_{j\in n}a_{ij}b_{jk}.$$

The sum is the finite sum in the additive commutative monoid of $F$. If $n=0$,
it is the empty sum, so $AB$ is the zero matrix of shape $m$ by $p$.

The **identity matrix** $I_n\in M_n(F)$ has entry $1$ when $i=j$ and entry $0$
when $i\ne j$. In particular, $I_0$ is the unique empty matrix in $M_0(F)$.

For $A=(a_{ij})\in M_{m\times n}(F)$, the **transpose** of $A$ is the matrix
$A^{\mathsf T}\in M_{n\times m}(F)$ defined by

$$(A^{\mathsf T})_{ji}:=a_{ij}.$$

Thus transposition interchanges rows and columns. The transpose of a zero-sized
matrix is the unique matrix of the transposed zero-sized shape.

Let $F$ be an ordered field ([[def-ordered-field]]) with positive cone $P$, and
let $a, b, c \in F$.

1. If $a > 0$ and $b > 0$ then $ab > 0$.
2. If $a > 0$ and $b < 0$ then $ab < 0$.
3. If $a < 0$ and $b < 0$ then $ab > 0$.
4. If $c > 0$ then $a < b \iff ac < bc$.
5. If $c < 0$ then $a < b \iff bc < ac$ (multiplication by a negative reverses order).

Let $d\ge1$ and let $G\in\mathbb R^{d\times d}$ be symmetric and positive semidefinite, meaning $v^\top Gv\ge0$ for every $v\in\mathbb R^d$. Then there is a unique symmetric positive-semidefinite matrix $H$ such that $H^2=G$. If $G=Q\operatorname{diag}(\lambda_1,\ldots,\lambda_d)Q^\top$ is an orthogonal diagonalization, this root is $H=Q\operatorname{diag}(\sqrt{\lambda_1},\ldots,\sqrt{\lambda_d})Q^\top$.

Let $F$ be a complete ordered field ([[def-complete-ordered-field]]). Then every
$a \in F$ with $a \ge 0$ has a **unique** $s \in F$ with $s \ge 0$ and $s^2 = a$;
we write $s = \sqrt{a}$. Consequently the positive elements of $F$ are exactly the
nonzero squares: $x > 0$ if and only if $x = y^2$ for some $y \neq 0$.
